2. The facts leading to the issuance of the Rule in a nutshell can be stated thus, the disputed property originally belonged to one Satindra Nath Roy Chowdhury under whom Umash Chandra Kayal, Akkya Chandra Kayal and Meghnath Kayal were tenants in equal shares. Meghnath Royal died leaving behind two sons namely, Kartik Koyal and Benimadhab Koyal, who inherited 2.02 acres of land each. Meghnath Koyal subsequently by amicable settlement with the co-sharers used to possess 1/3rd share to the extend of .17 1/3 acres of land in the suit plot no. 127 and in suit plot no. 126 he used to possess 3.86 ½ acres of land to the northern end of that plot. After the death of Meghnath Koyal Iris sons Kartik Koyal and Benimadhab Koyal made an amicable partition among them and in, pursuant to that Benimadhab obtained the land of suit plot No. 127. Kartik Chandra sold .69 acres of land from his share to one Shib Prashad Debnath, who subsequently transferred that land including his other land measuring 86, decimals of land in favour of the plaintiff's father Nirmal Chandra Mondal the present defendant no.4 on 05.08.1977. Thereafter, Kartik Chandra sold his rest 1.33 acres of land to the plaintiffs on 25.06.1982  but Kara Chandra subsequently exhausted his entire share of 2.02 acres of land in the suit Monza. For wand of dwelling but he could not shift immediately and requested the plaintiffs and their father to allow him to stay for a short term in 4 ½ decimals of land. The plaintiffs and their, father due to humanitarian consideration allowed Kartik Chandra to stay there for the time being till 30th Poush, of 1394 B.S. as licensee under them and executed an agreement on 2nd Kartik, 1390 B.S. corresponding to 20.10.1983 A.D. re tires effect. On 19.03.1985 the brother of Kartik Chandra, Benimadhab sold 16½ decimals of land to the defendant no.1 Babsilal but the plaintiffs after filing a pre-emption miscellaneous case obtained that land and thereby they acquired 1.49½ acres of land. Kartik Chandra died leaving behind the defendant nos. 1 and 2, who wore asked to leave the land measuring 4½ decimals as described in schedule 'Kira' of the plaint but they refused on 14.01.1988. Moreover, the defendant nos. 1 and 2 threatened the plaintiffs to oust them from the rest 1.45 acres of land and thereafter the plaintiffs filed the original suit for declaration of tide confirmation of possession and recovery of Khash possession in respect of 4 ½ decimals of land described in schedule 'Kha' of the plaint. 

 10. On perusal of the case record it transpires that admittedly the father of the defendant nos. 1 and 2 Kartik Chandra Koyal transferred the suit land in favour of the plaintiffs and the matter in dispute arose when the defendants claimed that the deed which was executed by Kartik Chandra was not a sale deed rather it was a mortgage with a condition to re-convey the suit land. Furthermore, admittedly the defendants are in possession in a particular portion of the suit land and that portion is 4½ decimals described in schedule kha of the plaint and in this context it is the contention of the plaintiffs that the defendants are licensee under them and that the defendants and prior to them their father Kartik Chandra was a permissive possessor under the plaintiffs in that portion of land. Beside this; having gone through the materials on record I find that the transfer deeds which has been marked as exhibit-1 and 1(A) dated 25.06.1982 and 27.07.1982 respectively are the documents upon which the plaintiffs banks. The learned appellate court below during disposal of the appeal rightly held that the deeds which were admittedly executed by the predecessor of the defendants were executed on two dates in the year 1982 as stated earlier but the alleged deed of agreement of re-conveyance which was marked as exhibit-B not executed on the same date in the same sitting. It is to be looked into whether exhibits-1 and 1(A) are sale deeds and whether the defendants are licensee in a portion of the disputed property described in schedule-`kha' of the plaint. The very contents of the documents go to show that the deeds are sale deeds and there is nothing to hold such a view that there was any talk to re-convey the land within the stipulated period of seven years. 

 12. It is obvious to note that the document for re-conveyance is to be executed in the same sitting at a time when the document is signed or executed and registered. Under the ambit of section 95A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act the learned appellate court below rightly pointed out the aforesaid legal aspect.
